paragraphs: (The biblical Evyatar son of Achimelech the priest is mentioned in I Samuel 23:7.) Hyman describes him as an amora in the Land of Israel in the third generation, a colleague of R' Yonatan (a student of R' Yochanan). As related in Gittin 6b, he sent Rav Chisda the ruling: “For bills of divorce brought from there to here, one need not say, ‘It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.’” Rav Yosef objected, “Who tells us R' Ivatar is a reliable authority? Moreover, he sent Rav Yehuda: ‘Those who go up from there to here have fulfilled of themselves, They gave the boy for a prostitute,’ and wrote it without ruled lines.” Abaye replied, “Does not knowing this ruling of Rabbi Yitzchak mean that someone is not a great man? Moreover, R' Evyatar is the one whose Master agreed with him.” R' Evyatar met Elijah and asked, “What is the Holy One, blessed be He, doing?” He answered, “Studying the concubine at Gibeah.” “And what does He say?” “My son Evyatar says this; My son Yonatan says this.” His statements occur in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 9:1; Bereshit Rabbah 48:12 and 88:2; Shemot Rabbah 1:29; Vayikra Rabbah 18:4; and Shir HaShirim Rabbah, chapter 7, verse 4.
And Hyman writes: We find that he had two sons, as is explained in Shevi'it ch. 6 halakhah 1, 18 (supplied: פ״ו ה״א-יח), where it says: 'the two sons of Avita of Dama.'

notes.text: The named Gittin6b text contains this exchange, rather than the supplied7b locator. Rabbi Yitzchak is spelled out in the adjoining ruling about ruled lines; Abaye’s question is about Evyatar’s ignorance of that rule, not Rabbi Yonatan’s greatness. The biblical priest is a namesake pointer only. The two sons’ Avita of Dama identification remains a source question.

The whole saved Guggenheimer Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit6:1 scalar, text index14 (504 characters), was read and checked against raw SHA256, selector and actual edition metadata. It has Rabbi Chiyya bar Wa asking the TWO SONS of Rabbi Evyatar of Dirmah. That full Rabbi title is local to the named Sheviit quotation only; it does not expand the heading or prove that this Evyatar is the man in the Gittin account. Hyman's supplied ב׳ בני אביתא דדמא remains the two sons of Avita of Dama, alongside the digital Evyatar/Dirmah reading, without replacing the supplied letters, harmonizing the persons/places, resolving paternity or asserting a corruption history. The source claim WE FIND HE HAD TWO SONS is expressly attributed and retains its definite wording and numeral, not automatically admitted as genealogy. The halakhah1 and trailing18 in פ״ו ה״א-יח are kept separately; they are not the range1-through18 or a verified18a folio. Other figures, priestly-travel/geographic boundaries and dialogue in the whole Sheviit scalar are not imported into the notice. The older Gittin6b and adjoining Yitzchak ruled-lines claims remain historical checked-context assertions in the carried note, not newly read whole named Gittin evidence this wake. The proposed body replacement of supplied7b by6b is not applied. R-Y in Abaye's question remains unexpanded, rather than transferring a full Rabbi Yitzchak title from an uninspected adjoining passage; older Yitzchak and mistaken Yonatan expansions remain exact in history. All unsupported abbreviated titles in the heading, Yonatan/Yochanan relation and Gittin Evyatar occurrences stay R'. Every explicit full Rav Chisda, Rav Yosef and Rav Yehuda remains Rav, while Abaye and Elijah stay untitled. The supplied single איבתר is distinguished as Ivatar from אביתר Evyatar, without a name harmonization or new identity binding. The opening biblical Evyatar son of Achimelech the priest is only Hyman's parenthetical namesake pointer; the source23:7 is preserved beside the old23:6-7 history without fresh biblical verification or a merger with the amora. Hyman's Israel/THIRD generation/colleague claim is expressly attributed, and the parenthetical STUDENT OF Yochanan stays attached to Yonatan without silently making Evyatar the student. FROM THERE TO HERE in both reports is retained without naming new locations. The divorce-report clause keeps NO NEED TO SAY and the two first-person IN MY PRESENCE formulations, not the earlier needless-to-say inversion or third-person paraphrase. The people GOING UP, THEY THEMSELVES/FULFILLED/BOY/FOR A PROSTITUTE, WITHOUT RULED LINES and both moreover clauses retain the source's force as reported quotations, not a new legal or moral ruling. The literal verse fragment is not expanded or supplied with an invented reference. WHO TELLS US reliable authority, DOES NOT KNOWING THIS R-Y RULING MEAN NOT A GREAT MAN, WHAT IS GOD DOING and WHAT DOES HE SAY remain genuine questions, with Abaye as questioner and Elijah as respondent. Master-agreed-with-him is the inherited contextual rendering of supplied דאסבים מריה ע״י, and He answered/studying are contextual renderings around supplied ע״ל; no Hebrew repair or printed reading is asserted. MY SON EVYATAR says thus/MY SON YONATAN says thus remains quoted speech, not a biological father relation. All statement locators retain their supplied chapter/section/verse distinctions: Berakhot9hal1, BR48section12 and88section2, Shemot1section29, Vayikra18section4, Shir7VERSE4; none are ranges or fresh named-edition mappings. All four original mixed notes, current mixed note, all English histories and root intermediate versions remain exact. Original note revision and source-resolution requests are not applied; only this qualification is appended and p002 remains held, without publication, canonical source repair, note retirement or semantic/authority admission.

The whole printed notice is in volume I, p. 98. It cites Gittin 7b; the whole corresponding exchange consulted here is at 6b, which the English now cites. The adjoining rule and Abaye’s question both explicitly name Rabbi Yitzchak, so that local R-Y is rendered Rabbi Yitzchak; this does not license a global expansion of similar abbreviations. Rav Yosef challenges Evyatar’s reliability, Abaye asks whether ignorance of a transmitted rule makes him less than a great man, and Evyatar asks Elijah what God is doing and saying. The fuller verse, fly/hair dispute and explanation of transmitted knowledge are not inserted into Hyman’s abridgement. “My son Evyatar” and “My son Yonatan” are quoted divine speech, not biological relationships. The single supplied Ivatar spelling remains distinct in the English, even though the consulted passage has Evyatar. The printed notice ends with “the two sons of Evyatar of Drama” (ב׳ בני אביתר דרמא), beside the frozen אביתא דדמא, rendered Avita of Dama. The whole Guggenheimer Sheviit 6:1 passage instead has Rabbi Chiyya bar Wa asking two sons of Rabbi Evyatar of Dirmah. These readings do not establish that this father is the Evyatar in Gittin, or identify the places. Hyman’s definite “we find that he had two sons” remains expressly attributed. The trailing 18 after halakhah 1 is retained separately, not converted to a range. The biblical priest remains a namesake pointer; the generation, colleague and other citation claims remain Hyman’s reported account. All Hebrew and existing notes remain unchanged. The retained notes describe earlier review stages; their pending-source statements are preserved as that record, alongside the new comparisons above.
